scratch_idea: The radian is the standard SI unit of angular measurement. It is defined as the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc length equal to the radius of that circle.
core_technique: Always ensure the angle is in radians before using the $S = r\theta$ formula.
check_questions: What is the SI unit of angular measurement?
How many degrees are in one radian?
What is the angular displacement in radians for one complete revolution?
common_pitfalls: Using degrees instead of radians in the arc length formula
Confusing the radius with the diameter when calculating radians

scratch_idea: Angular displacement is the angle through which an object rotates about a fixed axis. It is considered a vector quantity only for infinitesimally small values.
core_technique: Use the Right-Hand Rule to determine the direction: curl fingers in the direction of rotation, the thumb points along the axis.
check_questions: When is angular displacement treated as a vector quantity?
State the Right-Hand Rule for angular displacement.
What is the sign of angular displacement for counter-clockwise rotation?
common_pitfalls: Treating large angular displacements as vectors
Mistaking the direction of rotation for the direction of the vector

scratch_idea: Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement over time. It describes how fast an object is rotating and in what direction.
core_technique: Instantaneous angular velocity is a vector along the axis of rotation, following the Right-Hand Rule.
check_questions: Define instantaneous angular velocity.
What is the SI unit of angular velocity?
How do you calculate average angular velocity?
common_pitfalls: Confusing angular velocity with frequency (rev/s)
Ignoring the vector nature of angular velocity

scratch_idea: Angular acceleration is the rate at which the angular velocity of a rotating body changes. It occurs when a body speeds up or slows down its rotation.
core_technique: Angular acceleration is expressed in $rad \cdot s^{-2}$ and acts along the axis of rotation.
check_questions: Define angular acceleration.
What are the units of angular acceleration?
Does a body rotating at a constant speed have angular acceleration?
common_pitfalls: Confusing centripetal acceleration with angular acceleration
Forgetting that angular acceleration is zero for uniform circular motion

topic_name: Relation between Linear and Angular Velocity
scratch_idea: This concept links the speed of a particle moving along a circular path (linear velocity) to the rotational speed of the reference line (angular velocity).
core_technique: Linear velocity is always tangential to the circular path at any point.
check_questions: Derive the relation between linear and angular velocity.
What is the direction of linear velocity in circular motion?
Why is linear velocity in circular motion often called tangential velocity?
common_pitfalls: Assuming all points on a rigid body have the same linear velocity
Using the diameter instead of the radius in $v = r\omega$

scratch_idea: Tangential acceleration is the component of linear acceleration directed along the tangent to the circular path, representing the change in magnitude of linear velocity.
core_technique: Distinguish between tangential acceleration (changing speed) and centripetal acceleration (changing direction).
check_questions: Relate linear acceleration to angular acceleration.
Under what condition is tangential acceleration zero?
What is the direction of tangential acceleration?
common_pitfalls: Confusing tangential acceleration with centripetal acceleration
Assuming a point has zero acceleration if $\alpha = 0$ (it still has $a_c$)

scratch_idea: These equations describe the motion of a rotating body under constant angular acceleration, acting as direct analogues to the linear equations of motion.
core_technique: These equations only apply when the axis of rotation is fixed and $\alpha$ is constant.
check_questions: State the three equations of angular motion.
What linear variable is analogous to angular displacement $\theta$?
When can these equations be treated as scalar equations?
common_pitfalls: Using these equations when angular acceleration is not constant
Failing to convert initial values to SI units (e.g., rpm to rad/s)

scratch_idea: Centripetal force is the 'center-seeking' force required to keep an object moving in a circular path. It changes the direction of the velocity without changing its speed.
core_technique: Identify the physical source of centripetal force (e.g., tension, gravity, friction) in any given problem.
check_questions: What happens to a moving body if the centripetal force is suddenly removed?
Define centripetal force.
In what direction does the centripetal force act?
common_pitfalls: Thinking centripetal force is an 'extra' force rather than a requirement fulfilled by other forces
Mistaking centripetal force for centrifugal force

scratch_idea: The acceleration of an object moving in a circle, directed toward the center, caused by the continuous change in the direction of velocity.
core_technique: Centripetal acceleration is always perpendicular to the tangential velocity.
check_questions: What is the formula for radial acceleration in terms of angular velocity?
Why does a body moving with constant speed in a circle still have acceleration?
Calculate the radial acceleration if $v = 10 \text{ m/s}$ and $r = 2 \text{ m}$.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to square the velocity in the formula
Confusion between $a_c$ and $a_t$

scratch_idea: Banking involves raising the outer edge of a curved road to provide the necessary centripetal force through a component of the normal force, reducing reliance on friction.
core_technique: Banking allows vehicles to take turns safely at higher speeds even when the road is slippery.
check_questions: Why are highway roads banked at turns?
What provides the centripetal force for a car on a level road?
What determines the banking angle of a road?
common_pitfalls: Incorrectly identifying which force component provides $F_c$
Ignoring the role of friction on unbanked roads

scratch_idea: A device that uses high-speed rotation to separate substances of different densities. Denser particles move outward due to the lack of sufficient centripetal force.
core_technique: Heavier/denser particles require more centripetal force and thus settle at the bottom/outer edges if that force is not met.
check_questions: On what principle does a centrifuge work?
Explain how a cream separator works.
How does a washing machine dryer remove water from clothes?
common_pitfalls: Thinking the centrifuge 'pushes' particles out; it's actually their inertia and lack of $F_c$
Confusing the location of light vs heavy particles

scratch_idea: The minimum velocity required to put a satellite into a stable orbit near the Earth's surface.
core_technique: For low-flying satellites, the orbital radius is approximately equal to the Earth's radius ($R$).
check_questions: Define critical velocity.
Calculate the critical velocity of a satellite near Earth (Take $R=6400 \text{ km}$ and $g=9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$).
What is the approximate period of a low-flying satellite?
common_pitfalls: Using $g=9.8$ for satellites at very high altitudes
Incorrectly converting km to meters in calculations

scratch_idea: The general velocity required for a satellite to stay in orbit at a specific distance $r$ from the center of a planet.
core_technique: Note that orbital velocity is independent of the mass of the satellite.
check_questions: How does orbital velocity change as the distance from Earth increases?
Derive the expression for orbital velocity.
Does a heavier satellite require more speed to stay in the same orbit?
common_pitfalls: Using the satellite's mass in the orbital velocity equation
Confusing $r$ (distance from center) with $h$ (altitude above surface)

scratch_idea: Weightlessness occurs because the satellite and everything inside it are in a state of free fall toward the Earth, meaning no normal support force exists.
core_technique: Apparent weight is zero when the acceleration of the frame equals the local acceleration of gravity.
check_questions: Why do astronauts feel weightless in a satellite?
Is the gravitational force on an astronaut in orbit zero?
What happens to a spring balance reading inside an orbiting satellite?
common_pitfalls: Believing there is no gravity in space
Confusing actual weight ($mg$) with apparent weight (supporting force)

scratch_idea: Gravity simulated in a spacecraft by rotating it. The rotation creates a centripetal acceleration that mimics the sensation of weight for the inhabitants.
core_technique: The frequency of rotation must be adjusted based on the radius of the ship to match Earth's gravity ($g$).
check_questions: How can artificial gravity be created in a spaceship?
Derive the formula for the frequency of rotation to produce gravity $g$.
Where in a rotating spacecraft would the gravity be strongest?
common_pitfalls: Confusing frequency ($f$) with angular velocity ($\omega$) in the final result
Assuming gravity is created by the rocket's engines rather than rotation

scratch_idea: Moment of inertia is the rotational equivalent of mass. It measures an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion.
core_technique: Moment of inertia depends on both the mass and the distribution of that mass relative to the axis of rotation.
check_questions: Define moment of inertia.
What is the SI unit of moment of inertia?
Why is it harder to rotate a long rod about its end than its center?
common_pitfalls: Thinking moment of inertia is constant for a body regardless of the axis
Ignoring the $r^2$ factor in calculations

scratch_idea: This is the rotational version of Newton's Second Law ($F=ma$), stating that torque is the product of moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
core_technique: Use this formula to solve for angular acceleration when the applied turning force is known.
check_questions: Prove that $\tau = I\alpha$.
What is the rotational analogue of Newton's second law?
If the same torque is applied to two bodies, which one accelerates less?
common_pitfalls: Using linear mass instead of moment of inertia
Confusing torque with work or energy

scratch_idea: The rotational momentum of a particle, defined as the cross product of its position vector and its linear momentum.
core_technique: Direction is determined by the Right-Hand Rule of the cross product.
check_questions: Define angular momentum for a single particle.
What are the units of angular momentum?
When is angular momentum maximized for a moving particle relative to an origin?
common_pitfalls: Calculating it as a scalar without considering the angle $\theta$
Using the wrong reference point for the position vector $r$

topic_name: Angular Momentum of a Rigid Body
scratch_idea: The total angular momentum of a system of particles (rigid body) rotating about an axis, calculated as the product of moment of inertia and angular velocity.
core_technique: This formula is analogous to $p = mv$.
check_questions: Relate angular momentum to moment of inertia.
Does every point on a rigid body have the same angular momentum?
Show that $L = I\omega$.
common_pitfalls: Confusing $L$ with torque ($\tau$)
Using linear velocity instead of angular velocity

topic_name: Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
scratch_idea: If the net external torque acting on a system is zero, the total angular momentum of that system remains constant.
core_technique: When an object's moment of inertia decreases, its angular velocity must increase to conserve momentum.
check_questions: State the Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum.
How does a diver increase their spin rate in mid-air?
What happens to an ice skater's speed when they stretch their arms?
common_pitfalls: Applying the law when an external torque is present
Thinking kinetic energy is also conserved (it usually increases when $I$ decreases)

scratch_idea: Practical devices that use high angular momentum and moment of inertia to store energy and maintain orientation/stability.
core_technique: Large angular momentum makes a body resistant to changes in the direction of its axis.
check_questions: What is a flywheel used for?
How does a gyroscope maintain its orientation?
Mention two applications of gyroscopes.
common_pitfalls: Misunderstanding how stability is linked to angular momentum
Confusing the storage of rotational energy with torque
